extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy/history of science and scientists interested in the dynamics of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the significance, timing, and effects of scientific contributions (e.g., what makes a major vs. minor contribution; how paradigms and consensus shape research trajectories). Useful for assessing individual works, career episodes, or episodes of field development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude of adaptive modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude of phenotypic changes composing an adaptive walk should have an intermediate value—not so small as to be selectively insignificant, but not so big as to be almost certainly lethal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates from the Fisher/Kimura debate: very small changes are more likely to be favorable but have small fitness effects; large changes may yield larger fitness effects but are less likely to be favorable. Applicable analogically to scientific contributions: an effective change must be large enough to matter but not so disruptive as to be untenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-step dominance (inaugural-step importance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inaugural step in an adaptive walk accounts for, on average, a large portion of the total increase in fitness achieved during the ascent to a local optimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orr's results: the largest single-step increase during an adaptive walk is, on average, at least ~50% of overall gain. As an evaluative criterion, early contributions that produce large shifts are disproportionately significant to field progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric decline of contribution sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: The fitness contribution of particular adaptive modifications declines as an approximate geometric sequence: later steps are a constant proportion of previous steps and so become progressively smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies a characteristic historical pattern: one or two major early achievements followed by many smaller, diminishing 'mop-up' contributions. Use this to differentiate foundational vs. incremental work; figures (4.1–4.4) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiently unprecedented and sufficiently open-ended for paradigm-inducing works
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigm-inducing contributions share two essential characteristics: (1) their achievement is sufficiently unprecedented to attract an enduring group of adherents away from competing modes of activity, and (2) they are sufficiently open-ended to leave many problems for practitioners to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly drawn from Kuhn (quoted). Examples: Newton's Principia, Darwin's Origin, Lavoisier. When evaluating a claimed paradigm-shifting work, ask whether it both breaks with prior practice and generates a research agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to impose structure and produce consensus (paradigm adoption)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes just the reception of a paradigm that transforms a group previously interested merely in the study of nature into a profession or discipline; commitment and the apparent consensus it produces are prerequisites for 'normal science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contributions by their capacity to define standard methods, relevant phenomena, and to allow practitioners to locate themselves relative to the new framework (i.e., does the work structure practice space?). Quotations from Kuhn emphasize reception/consensus as causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foothold criterion (career-level high-magnitude early change)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively high-magnitude change early in a scientist’s career that gives a 'foothold'—a brief but highly resonant glimpse of a way forward—can define a research trajectory and lead to subsequent, smaller-scale elaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of footholds: finding a genuinely good research problem; perceiving the outline of a solution (e.g., Darwin reading Malthus). Use this to judge the career-significance of an event/insight: did it generate a sustainable research program?

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-selection as an evaluative skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a nose for a good problem—one that is sufficiently interesting, sufficiently difficult that it hasn't been solved, and ripe for solution—is a quality that distinguishes merely competent scientists from truly great ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess contributions and individuals by whether they select problems that yield rich, tractable research programs. Savas Dimopoulos's remark is cited as evidence of the centrality of problem-choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit of major changes to existing consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepting a major change to scientific practice during later stages of paradigm-governed research will require the community to divest itself of items of existing consensus; because of the high costs (revising a large body of existing knowledge), communities prefer smaller consistent modifications unless benefits outweigh costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed radical change, consider both the epistemic/organizational costs of discarding established consensus and whether the proposed benefits suffice to justify those costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range-of-evolvability / steering research directions
rubrics_metrics.description: A large initial step can carry a community much of the way to a particular optimum in practice space; once near that optimum, pursuing alternatives becomes costly and hence is precluded—so major contributions can 'attract an enduring group of adherents away from' other directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate whether a contribution narrows or channels future research trajectories (i.e., does it create an advertised path that excludes alternatives?). This explains occurrences of multiple independent discoveries and convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-paradigm diagnostic: lack of standard methods or fixed points
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a paradigm or candidate paradigm, facts that could pertain to a field seem equally relevant and fact-gathering is nearly random; contributions that define methods and standard phenomena remedy this state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works for their capacity to convert 'pre-paradigm' fragmentation into a coherent field by specifying shared problems, methods, and exemplars (Newton/Opticks example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness across scales (repeated re-scaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pattern of a big change followed by a geometrically decreasing series of smaller changes recurs at multiple scales: from large historical transitions to episodes within a scientist’s career (Orr's 'repeated re-scaling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing contributions, consider scale: the same evaluative dynamics (large early gains then smaller refinements) apply whether judging a field-wide revolution or a research program within one career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling-extreme-tail insight (rarity and impact of inaugural variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptive walks sample variants from the extreme right tail of a distribution; inaugural opportunities to increase 'fitness' (impact) decline in both frequency and magnitude as one approaches the optimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative heuristic, rare, extreme innovations early in a field's development are likelier to have outsized impact. This frames expectations about how often paradigm-scale contributions occur.
